direction:
Read the supplied script exactly, word for word, in one connected
performance. Do not add introductions, stage directions, commentary or any words.
This is a concise, warm, intelligent animated film for adult software developers.
Explain two diagrams as they build in front of an audience. The dependency tree
opens a question about construction order. The clockwise circle follows one
scenario, with observed progress and remaining work. Given, When and Then are
natural words, not spelled letters. Clearly distinguish a partial passing step
from the final result. Local failing test, passing test and refactoring feed back
into the wider check. Bring particular energy and clarity to five people working
together, splitting briefly into implementation and automation, and reuniting.
Cohesion and finishing have quiet conviction. The example is only a small aid to
understanding the process. Say AI as the letters A I. End with quiet assurance.
Use a fluent conversational pace around 160 words per minute. Retain natural
breaths, but avoid long dramatic pauses. No cartoon voices, announcer delivery
or imitation of Terry. Articulate 'displayed' with its ending. Finish the last
separate word, 'Together', fully; do not stop after 'scenario'. Only the script
is spoken.
script: Picture software as a tree: front end, back end, and smaller parts. It seems we must build from the bottom, then integrate upward. But assumptions about those parts can be wrong. We build things the result never needed. Instead, define one small end-to-end scenario with an automated test. Build enough to pass it; let the structure grow as needed. As it forms, useful internal tests can cover several lower parts together. Break a sprint item into small Given, When, Then scenarios. Each should satisfy a user need on its own. Here, we change a setting and check the displayed result. Take one scenario. Automate its first step using what already exists. Run it, and see it pass. Keep that executable evidence. The rest of the scenario is still unfinished. Add selection. Run it: the test fails because the dropdown is missing. We have evidence of the missing work. The earlier green step stays on the sheet. A temporary hard-coded dropdown gets us through sooner. Implementing it properly now is another choice. Either way, run the test again. The important result is still ahead. Add Update. If running it exposes a missing implementation, that failure tells us the next work. Follow it into the relevant logic. Protect the existing behavior we touch. Then use a local test: red, green, refactor. Repeat for the details this scenario needs. Return to the acceptance test. Now those earlier steps pass. But we still need Then. Add the result check and run it. The displayed result is wrong. Passing the actions did not finish the scenario. Five people have been working together. Once the next work is clear, three can implement the returned result, using a local test loop. Two can finish the acceptance automation at the same time. Both groups serve the same scenario. Then reunite, integrate, and run the complete acceptance test. All its steps pass together. Split for brief parallel exploration, and come back quickly. Done includes the required implementation and cleanup. Keep related domain concepts together from the beginning; make the structure coherent. Replace needed shortcuts under the checks. Finish the scenario completely. Only then take the next. There's also an advanced option: make Then real first, so the result is already observable. Earlier steps can begin as fakes and become real gradually. AI can help throughout this work, inside the scenario and its protective checks. Grow that scope deliberately. Acceptance Test Driven Development: work through one scenario.
